intro:
This is the audio overview of the JavaScript guide. JavaScript interviews return to the same small set of ideas again and again: closures, the keyword this, the event loop, and how values are compared and copied. If those four are solid, most questions are variations.

The guide has fourteen sections. Scope and closures, functions, async code and the event loop, data and equality, objects and prototypes, iterators and modules, and browser APIs. Then a compact look at TypeScript, TypeScript with React, and CSS. Then two deep dives, and a section of predict the output puzzles.

I will give you the rule behind each topic in plain words. The rules are what let you predict output without running the code.

chapters.title: Scope & Closures
chapters.text:
Section one is scope and closures.

A closure is what you get when a function remembers the variables from the scope it was created in, even after that outer scope has finished running. It is not a special feature you switch on. Every function does it. Closures are how you get private state, how a factory makes several independent counters, and how callbacks and event handlers know about the data they were set up with.

The classic bug is a loop with a timer. With var, every pass of the loop shares the same variable, because var belongs to the whole function. By the time the timers fire, the loop has finished, and they all see the final value. With let, each pass gets its own variable, so each timer sees its own number. The closure captures the variable, not the value.

Var, let and const. Var is function scoped and can be declared again. Let and const are block scoped. Const prevents you from reassigning the name. It is not immutability. An object or array that a const points to can still be changed.

Hoisting means that before a scope runs, JavaScript already knows its declarations. What differs is what you can do before the line is reached. A var reads as undefined. A function declaration can be called early. A let or const exists but cannot be touched, and trying throws an error. That stretch, from the start of the block to the declaration, is called the temporal dead zone.

chapters.title: Functions & Patterns
chapters.text:
Section two is functions and patterns.

Call, apply and bind all let you set what this refers to inside a function. Call invokes the function at once, with this and the arguments listed one by one. Apply also invokes it at once, with the arguments in an array. Bind does not invoke it. It returns a new function with this fixed for good, which you can call later. That is why bind is the one you use for callbacks.

Debounce and throttle both limit how often a function runs, in different ways. Debounce waits until the events stop for a set period, and then fires once. That suits a search box: wait until the person stops typing. Throttle runs at most once per interval while the events keep coming. That suits scrolling and dragging, where you want regular updates but not hundreds per second.

Debounce alone does not solve the stale response problem. Two requests can still be in flight, and the older one can arrive last. So cancel the previous request when a new one starts, or ignore any response that is not for the latest query.

Currying turns a function of several arguments into a chain of functions that each take one. Partial application fixes some arguments now and returns a function that takes the rest. They are useful for making specialised functions from general ones, such as a logger with its prefix already filled in, or an event handler that already knows which item it is for.

chapters.title: Async, Promises & Event Loop
chapters.text:
Section three is async code, promises and the event loop.

JavaScript is single threaded. One call stack runs one thing at a time. Async work does not block that thread. It is handed off, and its callback is queued for later. There are two queues. Microtasks hold promise callbacks and the code after an await. Macrotasks hold timers and events. The rule is: when the stack is empty, run all the microtasks, then take one macrotask. So a promise callback always runs before a timer, even a timer of zero.

A promise wraps a value that is not ready yet. It is pending, then either fulfilled or rejected, and it settles only once. Promises replaced deeply nested callbacks, where control flow and error handling became hard to follow.

To run independent operations together, choose by how you want failure treated. All gives you every result, and rejects as soon as one fails. All settled waits for everything and tells you which succeeded and which failed.

Two chaining mistakes come up constantly. Forgetting to return the inner promise from a then, so the chain moves on without waiting. And placing the catch where it does not cover what you think it does. An error travels down the chain to the first handler for rejections.

With try, catch and finally, the finally block runs whatever happens. And a try only catches an async error if you await inside it.

To cancel a request or add a timeout, use an abort controller. Aborting rejects the promise with an abort error, which you treat as control flow, not as a failure. It stops the browser's request. The server may still have done the work.

chapters.title: Data, Equality & Arrays
chapters.text:
Section four is data, equality and arrays.

Strict equality, the triple equals, compares both value and type with no conversion. Loose equality, the double equals, converts the operands to a common type first, and that is where the surprises live. An empty string equals zero. Null equals undefined, and nothing else. The practical rule is to use strict equality always. The one accepted exception is comparing loosely with null, to catch both null and undefined in one check.

And one value is not equal to itself: not a number. Test for it with the dedicated check.

Map, filter and reduce each return a new value, so you can chain them into one readable pipeline. Filter keeps some items, map transforms each one, and reduce folds them into a single result, such as a total. For very large arrays, remember that each step walks the whole array, and a single loop may be kinder.

Object or Map? Reach for a Map whenever the keys are not known ahead of time, are not strings, or the collection has entries added and removed often. A Map keeps insertion order, knows its size, accepts any value as a key, and has no inherited keys to trip over. A plain object is right for a fixed record with known fields.

A WeakMap holds its keys weakly. If nothing else in the program refers to a key object any more, the garbage collector may reclaim it, and the entry disappears. That makes it the right tool for attaching private data or cached results to objects you do not own, without causing a memory leak.

chapters.title: Objects, Prototypes & this
chapters.text:
Section five is objects, prototypes and this.

Every object has an internal link to another object, its prototype. When you read a property that is not on the object itself, the engine follows that link and looks there, then on that object's prototype, and so on up the chain until it finds the property or runs out. That is prototypal inheritance. Methods live once, on the prototype, and every instance finds them through the chain. The class syntax is a cleaner way of writing the same mechanism.

How is this determined? By how a function is called, not where it is written. Called as a method of an object, this is that object. Called as a plain function, this is undefined in strict mode. Called with new, this is the fresh object. Called through call, apply or bind, this is whatever you passed. The exception is the arrow function. It has no this of its own, and takes it from the surrounding scope. That is why arrow functions are convenient for callbacks inside methods, and wrong as methods themselves.

Copying. Spread makes a shallow copy: the top level is new, and nested objects are still shared. Converting to JSON and back makes a deep copy, but it loses dates, undefined values, functions, and anything circular. Structured clone is the built in deep copy, and it handles dates, maps, sets and cycles.

And for immutable updates in React or Redux, do not deep clone at all. Copy only the path you are changing, and leave everything else shared.

chapters.title: Iterators, Generators & Modules
chapters.text:
Section six is iterators, generators and modules.

An iterator is any object with a next method that returns a value and a flag saying whether it is done. An iterable is an object that can hand you an iterator. Arrays, strings, maps and sets are all iterable, which is why a for of loop and the spread syntax work on every one of them. The protocol is what those language features are built on.

A generator is a function that can pause. Each time it yields, it hands out a value and stops, and it carries on from that point when the next value is requested. That makes it lazy. It produces values one at a time, on demand, so it can describe a very long or even endless sequence without building it in memory. Generators suit reading pages of results one by one, and walking a tree. The async form lets you loop over data that arrives over time, such as a stream.

Then modules. CommonJS is the older system in Node. You call require, it runs synchronously, and it can be called anywhere, even inside a condition. ES modules are the standard. Imports and exports are static, declared at the top level, so tools can analyse them without running the code.

Two points to remember for interviews. ES modules have a static structure, which is what makes tree shaking possible: unused exports can be dropped from the bundle. And they have live bindings: an import is a view of the exporting module's variable, not a copy of its value. Together those also make circular imports behave predictably.

chapters.title: Browser APIs & DOM
chapters.text:
Section seven is browser APIs and the page.

An event travels in three phases. Capture, down from the window to the target. Then the target itself. Then bubble, back up through the ancestors. Listeners run in the bubble phase by default.

Event delegation uses bubbling. Instead of attaching a listener to every row of a list, you attach one to the list, and work out from the event which row was clicked. That is one listener instead of thousands, and it keeps working for rows added later. Two things to know: you can stop an event from travelling further, and a few events, such as focus, do not bubble.

A Web Worker runs JavaScript on a separate thread, so heavy computation does not freeze the page. The main thread keeps handling input and painting. A worker cannot touch the page directly. It has no access to the document. You talk to it by posting messages, and the data is copied, or transferred, between the two sides. Use one for parsing large files, image processing, or heavy calculations.

The intersection observer tells you when an element enters or leaves the viewport, or another container, without listening to scroll events. So it is efficient. It drives three common features. Lazy loading: only load an image when it is about to appear. Infinite scroll: put a marker element at the bottom of the list, and fetch the next page when it comes into view. And tracking whether something was actually seen. For images, there is also a simple built in attribute for lazy loading that needs no script at all.

chapters.title: TypeScript Fundamentals
chapters.text:
Section eight is TypeScript fundamentals, in brief.

Why use TypeScript when JavaScript exists? It adds static type checking, better editor tooling, safer refactoring and clearer contracts between pieces of code, and it compiles down to plain JavaScript. The types are gone at run time.

A tuple is a fixed length array type where each position has its own known type. Position carries meaning, like a pair of coordinates, or the value and setter that a state hook returns.

Generics let a function, a class or a type postpone choosing a concrete type until it is used. They are a type safe placeholder: one function, many types, and no loss of information.

Type alias or interface? A rule many teams use: an interface for the shape of an object or class that may need extending later, and a type alias for unions, tuples and everything else.

Pick and Omit both derive a new type from an existing one without declaring it again by hand. Pick is an allowlist: keep only these keys. Omit is a blocklist: everything except these.

Any switches type checking off for a value. Unknown is the type safe counterpart. It accepts anything, and you must narrow it before you use it.

Mapped types build a new type by looping over the keys of another. Conditional types choose a type with a test. Together they are how the built in utility types are written.

And for a fixed set of values, default to a union of string literals, or a constant object when you also need the values at run time.

chapters.title: TypeScript with React
chapters.text:
Section nine is TypeScript with React, four questions.

A reusable component, such as a select, should be generic. The type of its options flows through to the argument of its change handler. Pass it a list of users, and the handler receives a user. Nothing falls back to any, and the person using the component writes no type annotations at all.

Discriminated unions model props that depend on each other. One shared literal field, the discriminant, tells the compiler which of the other props are valid. Say an alert is either dismissible, and then needs a close handler, or not, and then must not have one. Written as a union, the invalid combinations do not compile. That is what people mean by making invalid states unrepresentable.

Then deriving types instead of duplicating them. There are utility types that give you the props of any component or native element. They are useful any time a component wraps another one. Your button accepts everything a native button accepts, plus a variant, and you never copy a list of attributes. The satisfies keyword checks that a value fits a type and still keeps its precise, narrow type.

Finally, the function component type against a plain function. Plain function declarations are the modern default. The older type used to add a children prop implicitly to every component, including ones that should not accept children, and it handles generics poorly. Typing the props parameter directly is simpler and more accurate.

chapters.title: CSS: Box Model & Positioning
chapters.text:
Section ten is CSS: the box model and positioning.

Every element is four nested boxes. From the inside out: the content, which is the text or image itself. The padding, which is space inside the border and takes the element's background. The border. And the margin, which is space outside the border, transparent, between this element and its neighbours.

How the width is counted depends on the box sizing setting. With content box, the default, the width is the content only, and padding and border are added on top. With border box, the width includes padding and border, which is far easier to reason about, so most projects set it everywhere.

One behaviour worth naming: vertical margins between neighbouring blocks collapse. The larger of the two wins, and they do not add up.

Then positioning. Static is the default, the normal flow of the page, and offsets do nothing. Relative keeps the element in the flow and lets you nudge it, and, more importantly, makes it the reference point for positioned children. Absolute takes the element out of the flow and places it against its nearest positioned ancestor. That is how you pin a badge to the corner of a card. Fixed places it against the viewport, so it stays put while the page scrolls, like a header or a chat button. Sticky behaves as relative until the page scrolls to a threshold, and then it sticks, like a table header that stays visible. Sticky needs an offset, and it only works within its scrolling container.

chapters.title: CSS: Selectors, Responsive & Animation
chapters.text:
Section eleven is CSS selectors, responsive design and animation.

Combinators describe the relationship between two selectors. A space means a descendant at any depth. A greater than sign means a direct child only. A plus sign means the very next sibling. A tilde means any later sibling. Mixing up descendant and child is a common source of styles applying to things you did not intend.

Specificity decides which rule wins when several match. Ids outrank classes, and classes outrank element names. When specificity is equal, the later rule wins. The practical advice is to keep specificity low and flat, mostly single classes, so that overriding a style never turns into a contest.

Responsive design is three things working together, not one trick. First, relative units, so sizes follow the user's settings and the container. Second, a layout that adapts by nature: Flexbox and Grid can wrap and share space with no breakpoints at all. Third, breakpoints for the cases where the layout really must change, written mobile first, so the base styles are for the smallest screen.

And animation. Why animate a transform, such as scale, instead of width or height? Animating layout properties forces the browser to redo layout: it recalculates the geometry of the element and everything around it, on every frame. Transform and opacity skip layout and paint. They are handled by the compositor, often on the graphics processor, so the animation stays smooth even when the main thread is busy. And respect the user's reduced motion preference.

chapters.title: Deep Dive: Async Puzzles & Patterns
chapters.text:
The first deep dive is async puzzles and patterns.

Event loop puzzles combine synchronous code, microtasks and macrotasks, and one order solves them all. All the synchronous code runs first. Then every microtask: promise callbacks, and the code after an await. Then one macrotask, such as a timer. Then all the microtasks again. Two details catch people. The function you pass when creating a promise runs synchronously, straight away. And an async function runs synchronously up to its first await. Only what follows the await is deferred.

Implementing debounce and throttle properly means more than the basic version. A good debounce offers cancel, so a pending call can be dropped when a component unmounts, and a leading edge option, which fires at the start of a burst instead of the end.

The most common async mistakes in real code. Awaiting independent operations one after another, when they could run together. Using an async callback in a for each loop, which does not wait. Forgetting an await, so an error escapes the try block. And a promise that nobody handles. The interview tip from the guide: if you are asked to speed up slow code, look for serial awaits of independent work first. It is the most common easy win.

Finally, designing errors. Subclass the built in error, so that instance checks and stack traces work, and set a name for readable logs. Use the cause option to wrap a low level error in a meaningful one without losing the original. And an aggregate error carries several failures at once, which is what you get when every promise in a race for the first success fails.

chapters.title: Deep Dive: Objects & Internals
chapters.text:
The second deep dive is objects and internals.

A Proxy wraps an object and lets you intercept operations on it: reading a property, writing one, deleting, checking whether a key exists, calling a function. Reflect is its companion, a set of functions that perform the default behaviour, so that your handler can do its extra work and then carry on as normal. Proxies are how reactive frameworks notice a change to your state, and they are used for validation and logging.

Every property has a descriptor. It says whether the property can be written, whether it shows up when you loop over the object, and whether it can be reconfigured or deleted. Three functions lock an object to different degrees. Prevent extensions stops new properties being added. Seal does that and also stops properties being removed. Freeze does both and makes the existing values read only. All three are shallow. A nested object inside a frozen object can still be changed.

The newer array methods return a new array instead of changing the original: a sorted copy, a reversed copy, a copy with one element replaced. They fit React and Redux well, where you must not mutate. A reminder that applies to both the old and the new sort: with no comparison function, items are compared as strings, so ten sorts before two. There is also a built in way to group an array's items by a key.

Last, memory leaks in the browser. The usual causes are listeners that were never removed, timers that were never cleared, caches that only grow, and references to elements that have left the page. To find one, repeat the suspect action many times, take heap snapshots before and after, and compare what was retained.

chapters.title: Predict the Output
chapters.text:
The final section is twenty four predict the output puzzles. You need the code in front of you to do them, so here are the rules they test.

Six are about the event loop. Synchronous code first, then all microtasks, then one timer at a time. A promise callback beats a timer of zero. An async function runs synchronously until its first await. And the function passed to a new promise runs at once.

Four are about scope. With var in a loop, timers all see the final value. With let, each sees its own. Reading a var before its line gives undefined. Reading a let before its line throws. A function declaration can be called before it appears. A function expression assigned to a variable cannot.

Five are about this. A method copied into a variable loses its object. An arrow function inside a method keeps the method's this, and a regular function inside it does not. Once a function is bound, calling it with another object does not change this. And a class method passed as a callback loses its instance.

Four are about values. Plus with a string joins text, and minus converts to numbers. Not a number is not equal to itself. The type of null is object. And the default sort compares as strings.

The rest are about promises and copying. A then that throws rejects the chain, and a catch that returns a value puts the chain back on the success path. All rejects on the first failure, and all settled never rejects. A try without an await does not catch. And a spread copy is shallow.

Work through them at a desk, and say the rule before you look at the answer.
